Background and Motivation

The increased power production from Variable Renewable Energy Sources (VRESs) creates a need for demand-side balancing [1]. To support grid balancing, end users must be flexible and adjust their power consumption to match changes in production and local grid conditions. One way to achieve flexibility is by adjusting consumption based on varying electricity prices, called Price-Based Demand Response (DR), as the electricity price reflects the current grid status. Additionally, emerging markets enable Incentive-Based DR participation by altering, often reducing, the power consumption upon request from a Distribution System Operator (DSO) or another enabler.

text: Objective and Contributions

The objective of this thesis is to develop an optimization model in Python to assess how an Energy Community (EC) can operate cost-efficiently, and also support the local DSO in relieving grid strain. This is done by scheduling a shared BESS and smart EV charging in response to Price- and Incentive-Based DR signals. Price-Based DR reduces operational costs in the EC by shifting electricity consumption to hours with lower electricity prices. It can also lower the demand charge of the grid tariff by minimizing the monthly peak consumption. Further, participation in an Incentive-Based DR program allows the DSO to request the EC to limit power consumption to support the grid when strained or unbalanced. To avoid rebound issues after a period of load reduction, the EC proposes solutions of controlled load shifting, referred to as temporal redistribution. This allows the DSO to choose predefined time slots to shift the load to, given the predicted rebound effects and the associated costs of this flexibility service.

Limitations

This thesis utilizes historical data at an aggregated level. The operational costs are calculated at a common metering point of the EC, and do not reflect the individual consumption. Only operational costs are considered, an investment cost analysis and remuneration schemes are excluded to focus on short-term flexibility and system operation rather than long-term economic feasibility. The results of the temporal redistribution are limited to model feasibility. A recommendation to the DSO regarding the optimal temporal redistribution is not provided, as this would require a detailed description of the grid, which is outside the scope of this thesis.

text: Transmission

The transmission grid functions as the motor highway of the power system. It consists of high-voltage lines operating between 132 kV to 400 kV [21]. These lines transfer power from power plants to various regions within the country and abroad through interconnections. The Transmission System Operator (TSO) in Norway is Statnett. Statnett is responsible for building, maintaining, operating, and stabilizing the transmission system during power imbalances to prevent system collapse [22]. The transmission system is a natural monopoly because building multiple parallel lines is economically irrational. Consequently, the TSO operates under strict regulations by the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE), ensuring the benefit of society and incentivizing innovation, optimal operation, and maintenance of the system. Some of the issues today on the transmission level include congestion and balancing challenges, which are costly [23]. The increased share of VRES raises the need for flexibility and balancing of the grid [16]. Currently, the load on the transmission grid is unevenly distributed, causing line capacity ratings in certain regions to be periodically challenged. Reinforcement efforts cannot keep up with the demand growth, meaning that these grid issues may persist. Future production and demand planning must account for the geographical distribution of generation and consumption, alongside flexible operation, to solve these challenges.

text: Distribution

The distribution grid transports power from the transmission grid's point of attachment to the end users [24]. It operates at a lower voltage level than the transmission system, ranging from 132 kV down to 230 V. The distribution grid is managed locally by a designated Distribution System Operator (DSO). The responsibilities of the DSOs include maintaining and improving voltage stability [3], which may be achieved by upgrading lines, transformers, or both [25]. Like the transmission system, the distribution network is a regulated monopoly. The Norwegian Energy Regulatory Authority (RME) ensures that the DSOs complies with the legal requirements and limits profit to ensure sensible operation of the grid [26].

text: The Energy Markets

The energy markets facilitate the purchase and sale of energy and power by connecting producers, retailers, traders, TSOs, and large-scale end users on common platforms [30]. Participants interact via market exchanges and by contracts, forming a complex yet organized system. Energy markets aim to balance power production before dispatch [31], however, due to uncertainties and natural fluctuations, they also include mechanisms to make real-time adjustments. Several energy markets exist depending on the time horizon and utility traded. Understanding how they operate is essential for comprehending the current role of flexibility, how it is marketed, and functions financially and physically.

text: The Day-Ahead Market - Elspot

The day-ahead market determines the generation schedules and power prices for the following day. In Norway, this market is called Elspot and is operated by Nord Pool [34]. Norway is divided into five price zones, as shown in Fig. 2.2.2, which may have different prices due to line transfer capacities between areas [35]. Producers in each area estimate production costs [36], including factors like weather, CO2-prices, and salaries, while retailers forecast the consumers' demand and willingness to pay. Both submit anonymous bids with price, quantity, and time for the following day. Daily at noon, Nord Pool matches supply and demand to determine the zonal prices using a "pay-as-cleared" method.

The Intraday Market - Elbas

The intraday market allows participants to trade energy continuously after the day-ahead market is closed [37]. For Norway, this market is called Elbas, and it is operated by Nord Pool. The market is open until one hour before dispatch, allowing for adjustments based on updated forecasts or unplanned events, thereby enhancing economic efficiency and grid stability [38]. In contrast to the day-ahead market, it is a continuous market where the lowest price offers are prioritized [37].

text: Grid Re-dispatch

After the closure of the intraday market, the TSO conducts load flow calculations to identify upcoming bottlenecks [40]. To mitigate these, the capacity market's bids are used to instruct market participants to adjust their production or consumption. The affected participants are compensated for their adjustments. While not a market in itself, grid re-dispatch plays a crucial role in power flow scheduling by ensuring security of supply and minimizing the need for capacity activation. Additionally, consumer flexibility may contribute to mitigating congestion [41].

text: Grid Tariff

The grid tariff is a charge payed to the DSO to cover the cost of transporting energy from a power producer to the end user. The tariff consists of three key elements: energy costs, power costs, and government fees [43].

text: First, the end users have a volumetric cost based on the amount of energy supplied to the end user, measured in [NOK/kWh]. The cost is typically higher during the day (06:00 - 22:00) than at night (22:00 - 06:00). Second, the end user is charged for their peak power demand [kWh/h] within the month, called the demand charge. For private consumers, the demand charge was implemented in 2022 to incentivize a more effective utilization of the grid [44]. Today, the charge is calculated by averaging the three highest hourly peaks within a month. The resulting value determines the cost according to predefined price brackets of power demand set by the local DSO. Higher simultaneous power consumption results in increased system losses [23] and thereby increased costs for the DSO. The third and last element of the grid tariff is the government fees [45]. The fees include Value Added Tax (VAT), an electricity tax to the government, and the Enova fee to the Climate and Energy Fund.

text: Flexibility

Flexibility relates to actively coping, overcoming, and adapting to changes from standard operation while maintaining desired performance [46], however, an agreed-upon and unified definition of flexibility does not yet exist [47]. The scope of flexibility in this thesis is how end users, represented by an EC, adapt to deviations from optimal operation while ensuring power reliability and cost efficiency. These deviations must not come at a loss of comfort for the end users [48]. Today, end users generally have limited knowledge and resources on flexible energy usage. Meanwhile, the increasing share of VRES makes balancing the power system more challenging. Thus, consumers must become more flexible and adjust their energy consumption in line with production to maintain system balance [1].

text: Demand Response

Building on DSM, DR refers to activities and programs that influence or motivate when and how energy is consumed through dynamic pricing, advanced metering, and other enabling technologies [51]. End users who are flexible with their power usage, energy usage, or both, fit into one of two categories. The first is Price-Based DR, and the second is Incentive-Based DR. text: Price-Based Demand Response

With Price-Based DR, the end users are motivated to voluntarily adapt either their power or energy usage, or both, in line with price signals to reduce costs [1]. One of these signals may be the spot price. Power prices are generally lower during periods of sufficient power production and bidding zone transfer capacity. This encourages consumers to increase their demand during these hours. In contrast, power prices are higher during periods of limited production or transfer capacity between bidding zones. High prices encourage consumers to reduce their demand during these hours. Another price signal is the demand charge. This price signal focuses on evening out energy consumption and lowering peak power demand, as this lowers the cost.

text: 2.4.2.2 Incentive-Based Demand Response

For Incentive-Based DR, the aim is to motivate end users to alter their power consumption upon requests from their DSO, TSO, or any other flexibility service provider [1]. The goal with this is to aid grid operators in voltage, frequency, or congestion problems, or a combination of these. When restricting power import, consumers may be remunerated based on how far in advance the signal is sent and the amount of load reduction [52]. In contrast to Price-Based DR, end users must actively participate in Incentive-Based DR activities. The consumption of the end users is altered to improve the current or future state of the grid, which is possible without any loss of comfort for the end users [48].

text: Flexibility Potential of End Users

In Incentive-Based DR, end users adjust their power consumption, energy consumption, or both, in exchange for economic compensation [49]. The amount of load an end user can adjust is known as their Flexibility Potential (FP). The amount of FP is a fundamental element when determining the level of activation and remuneration for the end users [53]. The end user's baseline consumption represents their expected load curve in the absence of any external influences [53], as illustrated in Fig. 2.4.2. It is typically estimated using historical data or various predictive modeling techniques [54]. In contrast, the metered load is the actual load curve observed in real-time when the end user actively adjusts their consumption in response to an Incentive-Based DR signal. The FP is calculated by measuring the difference between the actual metered load and the estimated hypothetical baseline load over the service duration [54]. A challenge in determining the remuneration of FP is that consumers may exploit the baseline calculation into make it appear higher than it actually is, thereby increasing their remuneration [53]. On the other hand, the calculation method may also allow the responsible party to underpay participants. This highlights the importance of using a robust method when calculating baseline consumption.

text: Rebound Effect

A rebound effect occurs when electrical loads that were temporarily turned off or used less power, such as during an Incentive-Based DR event, return to their normal operation all at once [6]. This sudden surge in power consumption can lead to unintended frequency problems in the grid [6]. Additionally, if it is known that power consumption will be reduced in the future, consumption may increase in advance to prepare for this. This behavior can be considered a rebound effect resulting from proactive countermeasures. The rebound effect has been documented in several studies [55].

text: Energy Communities

To the authors' knowledge, there is no uniform definition of the term "Energy Community" (EC). Recurring elements in the literature describe local communities that together contribute to the green transition, providing environmental, economic, or social benefits through conscious electricity consumption [58]. The European Commission has derived its definition through the EU's Clean Energy for all Europeans package [59]. It emphasizes that an EC should be an open and voluntary entity, controlled by its members or shareholders, with the goal of providing local community benefits rather than solely maximizing financial profits through different energy services. Two directives within this package specifically mention ECs: Directive 2018/2001 (RED II) [60], which outlines the characteristics of energy communities, and Directive 2019/944 (IMED) [29], which describes the markets in which they should operate.

The primary aim of the study is to coordinate the BESS to improve voltage at the distribution level. The study finds an optimal BESS modeling that results in fewer voltage spikes and no cases of overvoltage. Operating in a battery-degradation-friendly way increases the lifetime of the BESS, postponing battery replacements and the costs that follow because of this. Emphasis is put on optimizing for the demand charge, as this could lower peak consumption further and result in fewer grid issues.

text: Linear Programming

In linear programming, both the objective function and the constraints consist of linear expressions. It is one of the most important mathematical methods used in operations research [79]. The objective function defines what is to be maximized or minimized. In the energy sector, typical objectives are minimizing power losses or maximizing profits [79]. Constraints capture the problem's physical and operational limits, such as conservation of energy, BESS operation, and EV charging requirements. They define the feasible region of possible solutions by limiting resources and controlling the interactions between variables. The unknowns to be determined are called variables, often organized into sets when there are multiple variables involved. The coefficients are known as model parameters.

text: Time-adaptive Optimization

In time-adaptive optimization, the optimization model simulates decision-making over time by allowing for input data to be updated or revealed. The optimization model is then able to react to the new information, selecting the optimal solution based on the available input data. Two methods that implement this feature are the Rolling and Receding Horizon frameworks.

text: Rolling and Receding Horizon

Rolling Horizon and Receding Horizon are optimization frameworks that allow for the inclusion of time dynamics in the simulation. This is achieved by iteratively solving the optimization model in predefined time stages, and allowing for updates in the input data to be made during execution [80]. text: Both Rolling and Receding Horizon are dependent on defining three different time horizons. The first is the scheduling horizon (SH). This is the entire period the optimization model is run. The next horizon defines how much information the model is given in each iteration, i.e., the available information. This is referred to as the prediction horizon (PH), and the length of this depends on the selected method. The information given in the PH can be updated at each time step. Lastly, the control horizon (CH) is defined as the time unit of optimization. This is what is solved and stored before moving on to the next iteration [80].

text: Multi-stage Stochastic Programming

A multi-stage optimization problem is solved sequentially over several stages. Decisions at one stage influence the outcome and costs in future stages. The variables linking decisions across stages are known as state variables [83]. Their values must be transferred between stages, as the outcome of one stage becomes the input for the next. For example, the State of Charge (SoC) of a BESS at the end of a day is used as the initial SoC for the next day. In stochastic programming, uncertainty is included in the optimization model to handle random or unknown parameters. This approach allows for a more realistic representation of real-world situations and enables the use of future predictions as input data. By combining these concepts, it allows for modeling systems where decisions are made over time, and each stage presents new stochastic information. Several methods handle multi-stage stochastic problems well, one of which is the SDDP method [83].

text: Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming

SDDP is a method for solving large multi-stage optimization problems using dual solutions to approximate the expected-cost-to-go function, which conveys information between stages. The stages are decomposed and solved iteratively through so-called forward and backward passes until convergence is achieved and a final solution is obtained. This method avoids the use of discretization of state variables, and the "curse of dimensionality" is mitigated. Also, the method manages stochastic problems well. A drawback of the method is that the problem must be convex [83].

text: A key challenge of solving multi-stage optimization problems is not only transferring the value of the state variables, but also capturing the future impact of current decisions [83]. A solution that appears optimal when considering a single stage may be suboptimal when evaluated with respect to all stages. For example, a battery might discharge completely at the end of the day to avoid wasting energy. However, a more optimal solution might be to store some energy for the following day. SDDP uses the expected-cost-to-go function as a means to communicate this information between the stages.

text: Summary

Updating input data through Rolling and Receding Horizon frameworks adds adaptability to short-term scheduling, allowing the system to respond dynamically to new information when it becomes available. However, long planning horizons are computationally demanding and depend on possessing all the future information needed, limiting their practicality. For this thesis, a shorter, dynamically updated planning horizon is more realistic and effective. While Rolling and Receding methods performs well in short-term adaptability, they do not account for long-term uncertainty. SDDP offers a valuable complement, especially in systems involving multiple state variables. Combining SDDP with Rolling and Receding Horizon approaches enhances the overall performance by integrating the ability to convey long-term operational consequences with the agile responsiveness in short-term operation.

text: Model Description

The goal of the optimization model is to reduce the operational costs of an EC concerning the energy supply over a month, by following Price-Based DR signals. The costs considered here are the varying spot price and the grid tariff. Thus, optimal scheduling of EV and BESS charging is necessary to shift high loads to hours with low pricing, while still keeping the demand charge as low as possible. Additionally, the EC receives a signal from their local DSO with a request to lower the grid import for one hour. This is to simulate participation in an Incentive-Based DR program. The EC is also equipped with features to enable temporal redistribution of load in an Incentive-Based DR event.

text: Incentive-Based DR Signal

An Incentive-Based DR program may aim to reduce grid import during a specific hour, henceforth referred to as the "restricted hour". It is assumed that the EC participates voluntarily in such a program and must therefore be prepared to respond to reduction requests. A request signal, referred to as an Incentive-Based DR signal, is issued by the DSO or another enabling entity. The signal is received a certain time before the restricted hour. For example, notice times of 12 hours, 2 hours, 15 minutes, and 0 minutes are used in Glitre Nett's flexibility scheme [66] and in the work of [77].

text: Temporal Redistribution

During the restricted hour, the intended energy consumption for the EC must be shifted to other hours. Traditionally, this could result in shifting load to less cost-effective hours, in addition to risking shifting load to hours where consumption is already high, causing an increased demand charge. This results in a higher total cost of the EC. Additionally, this load shifting does not allow the DSO to foresee the possible grid issues caused by rebound effects. However, by shifting the energy to predefined periods, referred to as "blocks", the DSO can assess the implication of choosing one block over another, act proactively to mitigate rebound effects that may stress the grid and evaluate the resulting cost changes.

text: Algorithm

To schedule the operation of the EC, an optimization model is developed. As a consequence of the system being exposed to receiving new information during operation, such as an Incentive-Based DR signal, the model must support dynamic updates. To handle this, a combined RRH framework is implemented. However, since the demand charge is calculated based on the monthly peak, and the model only optimizes over a shorter period at a time, a mechanism is needed to account for the long-term effects of current decisions. This thesis uses the SDDP algorithm to generate expected-cost-to-go functions that capture and communicate the long-term consequences of operation.

text: Generating the Cuts Using SDDP

The main function of the SDDP method in this optimization model is to generate expected-cost-to-go functions that capture the long-term consequences of the three state variables' values. The first state variable in the optimization formulation is the monthly peak grid import, which determines the demand charge for the EC. The second and third are the SoC of the shared BESS and flexible EV charging, respectively. To fully utilize the battery, it is permitted to discharge additional energy or store extra charge into the following day. Optimizing across three state variables over a month can quickly become computationally intensive if not considered properly when selecting the method. Therefore, the SDDP methods are selected in this thesis to avoid the "curse of dimensionality" as a consequence of having three state variables. A major advantage of SDDP is its use of dual values to focus on the most relevant regions of the state space, thereby reducing the overall computational load. A drawback is finding the optimal operation strategy for the EC, as it does not account for the activation of an Incentive-Based DR signal.

text: Flow Chart

A flow chart of the algorithm is presented in Fig. 5.2.2. First, the SDDP algorithm is run to obtain the Benders cuts needed to create the expected-cost-to-go functions providing the long-term consequences of operation for each day in the model, except for the last. When the Benders cuts are acquired, the first planning horizon of the RRH framework is initialized and the iterations over the hours of the month begin. First, there is a check for an Incentive-Based DR signal. If a signal is received, marginal cost curves are created before a decision is made whether to activate the signal or not. If the signal is activated, the input data is updated with the necessary information. This includes the grid import reduction in the restricted hour, and also the desired temporal redistribution strategy selected by the DSO. Regardless of whether an Incentive-Based DR signal is received or activated, the current planning horizon is solved to obtain the solution to the control horizon. The next step is to check if the end of the scheduling horizon is met. If not, there is an additional check if the hour is 13:00. If this is true, the spot prices for the following day are revealed, and the planning horizon is extended, as shown in Fig. 5.2.1. Then, regardless of whether the planning horizon has been extended or not, the prediction horizon is reduced by one step, the iteration moves one hour forward, and there is a new control horizon to be optimized. This loop continues until the final control horizon has been analyzed.

This limits how much energy can be shifted to the next day. If not implemented, it is possible to charge all the EVs during the first days, ending up not having to charge them again for the remainder of the month, which is an unrealistic solution. text: Case Study
Case Study

The overall goal is to study how an EC with flexible resources can participate in an Incentive-Based DR program and avoid potential rebound effects, while reducing operational costs. The fictional EC studied is located in Trondheim, Norway. This corresponds with the prize zone NO3, and Tensio as the local DSO. The EC is modeled to consist of 25 households, a shared BESS, and smart EV charging. The Incentive-Based DR program aims to reduce grid power import for one hour of the month, and the load of this hour must be shifted elsewhere. To achieve this, various load shifting implementations are applied. How the BESS and EV charging are scheduled to overcome the restricted hour is of interest.

On January 7th (Fig. 7.1.1b, orange line), an increase of the peak power import from 60 kWh/h to 69 kWh/h has a marginal cost of zero. This indicates that grid import below 69 kWh/h does not affect the demand charge's cost as the model expects the peak grid import to be higher than this value later in the month. Beyond 69 kWh/h until 75 kWh/h, the marginal cost rises rapidly, reflecting the increased cost of having a peak import higher than 69 kWh/h. The actual cost of increasing the peak power import by 1 kWh/h is 36.48 NOK as this is the variable cost of the demand charge, as seen in Eq. 6.1. A marginal cost of less than 36.48 NOK is achieved by utilizing the increased peak to take advantage of spot price variations. Raising the peak earlier in the month allows for more possibilities of profiting from lower spot prices, and thereby a lower marginal cost. As the month progresses, the chances to take advantage of these price differences decrease. Consequently, the marginal cost of increasing the peak import typically rises from one day to the next. The marginal cost for January 31st (pink) stabilizes at 36.00 NOK/kWh/h, indicating low economic gain from increasing the peak power import on the last day of the month.

text: Operation

Fig. 7.1.2 displays three figures that show the dynamic behavior of the grid import and its allocation in the EC over four consecutive days. The figures show how the flexible resources operate to minimize the volumetric electricity costs, and the general effect the inclusion of the demand charge in the objective function has on the grid import. Each sub-figure provides a detailed hourly resolution of grid import (pink), household load (light gray), regular EV charging (dark gray) and volumetric electricity price (dashed gray). The operation of the EC is determined using the RRH framework, which performs hour-by-hour optimization with new information revealed daily at 13:00. SDDP cuts, as exemplified in Fig. 7.1.1a, are incorporated to inform the model of the long-term consequences of its daily decisions. Fig. 7.1.2a shows the operation of the EC without any flexible resources enabled. The increased grid import during high-price periods and reduced imports when prices are low suggest that the end users are not actively responding to price signals. This implies a lack of awareness in the consumption behavior. Fig. 7.1.2b displays the same days as in (a), however, now the flexible resources are active and respond to the varying volumetric electricity prices. This is seen by how the BESS discharges (red) when the volumetric price increases in the morning hours of January 5th and charges (light green) during the night hours with lower costs. In addition, EV charging is shifted (dark red) to avoid the more expensive hours, and additional charging (dark green) is scheduled in the low-price hours. The demand charge is excluded from the objective of the optimization problem, and the optimization model can freely utilize the spot price variations to lower the operational costs.

Lastly, Fig. 7.1.2c visualizes the behavior of the flexible resources with the demand charge included in the optimization formulation. Now the optimization model must weigh up the cost saved by utilizing low-price hours, with the cost of increasing the peak import and thereby also the demand charge.

When comparing Fig. 7.2.1a and Fig. 7.2.1b, two distinct strategies for managing the grid import restriction are revealed. In Fig. 7.2.1a, where the demand charge is excluded, the model simply reschedules the planned discharge of the BESS without concern for exceeding a specific peak. It is necessary to reschedule the operation of the BESS, as it is already on a tight schedule, to maximize the use of spot price variations. In contrast, Fig. 7.2.1b, which includes the demand charge, shows how the load is shifted to hours with lower grid import levels. Although these hours are previously avoided due to higher volumetric electricity costs, the optimization model concludes that utilizing them is more cost-effective than increasing the peak import. The BESS, in this scenario, is not operated at such a tight schedule, and the model can charge the BESS additionally to prepare for the necessary discharge by the charging performed in the hours right before and after the restricted hour.

section_title: Case 2 - Temporal Redistribution Before vs. After
text: In Case 2, temporal redistribution is introduced. Now, there are two options to manage the consequences of the restricted hour. The first is to prepare the flexible resources ahead of time. Changes to the grid import may only occur between the signaled hour and the restricted hour, and may not exceed the optimal grid import for the remainder of the day. This period is henceforth referred to as Before. The second option is to deal with the consequences and act reactively after the hour of restriction. Changes may only occur between the restricted hour and the end of the day. This period henceforth referred to as After. From the 7th and onward, the optimization model may freely modify the grid import, as the restriction scheduling on the 6th may have repercussions for the operation schedule for the remainder of the month.

Thus, the feasibility of participating in Incentive-Based DR programs and the choice of temporal redistribution depend on when during the day the restricted hour is set to be.

text: The plot shows that reducing the grid import, and thereby increasing the peak import, is more expensive towards the end of the month. This is because when a peak increase occurs early in the month, the operation schedule is adjusted for the rest of the month to take advantage of this new peak. If a peak increase occurs towards the end of the month, there are fewer hours to take advantage of the possible lower volumetric electricity cost. The large steps in the marginal cost occur at different grid import reductions because the possible grid import reduction before the peak grid import is increased varies from day to day. For instance, day 31 increases the peak grid import much earlier than day 2. This is solely due to the variations in daily operation in response to the price signals and consumption demand of that day. Note that the cost of increasing the peak power is constant, as it is simply a function of the demand charge in Eq. 6.1. It is the potential savings through the volumetric reductions that influence the overall marginal cost curves. These results indicate that not only does the time of day influence the cost of providing flexibility, but also the time of month.

Utilizing the extended SoC range of the battery comes at a penalty cost of 1 NOK/kWh, in addition to the spot price variations which will also affect the marginal cost. This is a value that may only be expected for the final days of the month. The reason for finding this value in the earlier days of the month may be a result of a weakness due to using the SDDP algorithm to make the future predictions. The algorithm of SDDP only looks at the interesting values of the state variables, as visualized in Fig. 7.1.1b. As the grid import reduction increases, making the peak import increasingly greater than the optimal value, the predictions of future consequences become more and more inaccurate. The reason day 6 does not reach the 14 NOK/kWh/h plateau is that, on this day, grid import can be reduced significantly before triggering an increase in peak grid import. Consequently, the peak is not raised as early as on other days, where the system is forced to increase the peak sooner. Thus, the predictions for day 6 are not pushed into the linear region of the graph (illustrated in Fig. 7.1.1a), and the expected-cost-to-go function remains accurate in this case.

text: Optimizing for the demand charge, rather than not, is the superior approach across all cases for several reasons. First, it leads to a lower total cost in every case. As the EC is naturally exposed to the demand charge, it gives a more comprehensive view of all elements affecting the total cost. For example, in Case 0, the demand charge is reduced by more than half, from 5212.39 NOK to 2594.45 NOK, when including the demand charge in the optimization problem formulation. As the costs are low for including the demand charge, it implies that the model never has to increase the peak grid import with this strategy.

text: The DSO's Perspective

Optimizing the EC's operation for the demand charge, and implementing temporal redistribution in response to Incentive-Based DR signals, simplifies the grid management for the DSO. The DSO benefits from stable grid operation. This enhances the grid efficiency and enables the integration of more users without compromising system stability or exceeding the power capacity.

text: Another valuable aspect for the DSO is having insight into the potential timing of rebound effects to support their operational planning. Throughout the cases, as the duration of temporal redistribution is shortened, the timing of the rebound effects becomes increasingly predictable. Case 1 and Case 2 exhibit similar rebound patterns. However, Case 2 provides additional insight by indicating whether the rebound occurs before or after the restricted hour. This information may be valuable for the DSO in anticipating the consequences of sending an Incentive-Based DR signal. Although Case 3 results in higher rebounds compared to Case 1 and Case 2, the duration of these effects is shorter, but predictable. The general trend across the cases is that a shorter time window to make adjustments is more expensive, and the impact of the rebounds is greater. Longer time windows can help minimize the increase in peak import and lower the rebound effects, though the exact timing is uncertain. From the DSO's perspective, this introduces a trade-off between rebound predictability and grid impact. The greater certainty in the timing of rebound effects is associated with increased intensity, while lower predictability tends to produce milder impacts.

section_title: The Use of SDDP to Capture the Long-Term Consequences
text: One of the main advantages of using the SDDP algorithm to create the expected cost-to-go function is its efficiency. This is a consequence of it only testing interesting values of the state variables, thereby avoiding the "curse of dimensionality." The expected cost-to-go function obtained is highly accurate around the optimal solution. However, this comes at the expense of reduced accuracy for values that fall outside this range. This can be seen in Fig. 7.1.1a, where ranges outside the interesting values are represented only by a straight line. If the state variables are pushed outside the optimal range, for instance by the activation of an Incentive-Based DR signal, the consequences would not be depicted as accurately as if the values stayed within the explored range.

section_title: The Use of SDDP to Capture the Long-Term Consequences
text: Another method used to convey the long-term consequences of multi-stage dynamic optimization problems is the Stochastic Dynamic Programming (SDP) algorithm. This method resembles SDDP in that it splits the optimization problem into individual stages and creates an expected-cost-to-go function. However, one of the main differences is that it does not iterate through forward and backward passes. Instead, it starts at the end and uses a discretization of the state space to test different values of the state variables. The information obtained is then used to convey the consequences in the previous stage, and so on. Consequently, the expected cost-to-go function is created for the entire range of tested state variables. This approach to solving the multi-stage optimization model allows for the use of non-linear equations. However, for this optimization problem, SDP would have quickly become very large, as there are three state variables and individual stages for each hour in the month. Additionally, the number of discretized values must also be determined. This involves a trade-off between accuracy and computational time. Furthermore, SDP is not as accurate near the optimal solution as SDDP.

text: Battery Degradation

When the demand charge is not factored into the optimization, the BESS and EVs may charge rapidly within a single hour, even when subsequent hours have the same volumetric cost. This behavior needlessly increases the demand charge and accelerates the degradation of both the BESS and the EV batteries. Charging at lower power over multiple hours is preferable, as it represents a healthier way of operating for flexible resources [3]. This issue is mitigated when the optimization accounts for the demand charge as the EC is incentivized to avoid large deviations in grid import across the hours. In addition, the applied penalty of 1 NOK/kWh for utilizing the full capacity of the BESS serves as a repercussion for increased battery degradation. However, this penalty does not capture the effects of rapid charging within the 20–80% SoC range. Including a comprehensive battery degradation model in the optimization could incentivize more deliberate and conscious use of flexibility resources, thereby improving their availability for participation in Incentive-Based DR programs. However, as discussed previously, this comes at the cost of using SDDP to convey the long-term consequences.

text: Feasibility of Smart EV Charging

In cases when it is optimal to shift EV charging from the daytime to the nighttime, the results assume that the EVs are physically connected to a charger during those hours. In reality, this is not always guaranteed, as the availability of plugged-in vehicles depends on user behavior. Without a sufficient number of EVs plugged into the charger, the planned load shift is impossible. In such cases, the charging must be carried out in higher-cost hours, or consequently, increase peak power import. Also, the charging periods are assumed to be full hours, while in practice, the times at which customers connect their vehicles are a fraction of an hour. By neglecting these real-world barriers, the resulting schedule may overestimate the achievable performance of the system and underestimate the operational costs, leading to a sub-optimal solution. An upside of fewer connected EVs is that the rebounds are smaller, as the total impact of the reactivation of charging is reduced. If the smart EV charging is extended to include vehicle-to-grid, then the presence of EVs is vital to provide the grid service. Because of these factors, these EC charging should be considered more conservative than what is found in the results.

text: Conclusion
Conclusion

This thesis investigates how flexible resources in an Energy Community (EC), with a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and smart Electric Vehicle (EV) charging, can participate in an Incentive-Based Demand Response (DR) program, while minimizing rebound effects and operational costs. A linear optimization model of the EC is developed using the Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming (SDDP) methodology combined with a Rolling-Receding Horizon (RRH) approach. The RRH framework simulates the daily revelation of spot prices, while the long-term consequences of operation is captured by the SDDP algorithm. A temporal redistribution strategy, providing controlled load shifting, aims to predict and mitigate the severity of rebound effects when reactivating curtailed loads. The loads are curtailed upon request by the Distribution System Operator (DSO), simulating an Incentive-Based DR event. Case 0 optimally schedules the EC's flexible resources for price signals, thus, the possible additional deliverable flexibility requested by the DSO is challenged. Three cases impose increasingly stricter limitations on temporal redistribution.
